comments.body: My problem with this opinion pieces—and of some of French’s assumptions—is that it seems like many conservatives equate a place where a multitude of different opinions run free as “liberal indoctrination”. I went to Harvard, graduated in 1995. I didn’t even know what politics any of my professors had. I didn’t even know what politics I had – or most of my fellow students had. Politics just didn’t matter much to us. We were interested in having debates and getting to the truth about things. Or at least coming to own conclusions about them. Topics included issues considered hot-button political footballs in the wider world: abortion, religion, American interventionism. But nobody was being indoctrinated. Our minds were being opened to myriad opinions from tons of bright young students and professors. I’ve had my issues with Harvard over the years—many of my fellow graduates can act arrogant and privileged. But anyone who has the opportunity and means to attend a school like Harvard should consider themselves lucky. I certainly do.

These interceptors could become one layer of a broader defense.

Imagine an imminent attack on a U.S. base, city, reservoir or power grid. Launchers could release thousands of drones, coordinated like a civilian light show but assigned defensive roles. Some detect threats through radar, radio and optical sensors. Others relay data, jam guidance or generate false radar and heat signatures based on chaff, flares and towed decoys. A final group intercepts incoming drones. Together, they form a shifting aerial web instead of firing one costly missile at each cheap target.

Pieces already exist. Interceptor drones are used against Shaheds in Ukraine and produced for Middle Eastern defenses. Autonomous formation flight has been demonstrated. Electronic warfare disrupts drone communications and navigation; ground-based lasers and high-powered microwaves are being tested. The next step is integrating them into a network. Powerful lasers should remain mainly on land or ships, where energy and cooling are available, while drones supply targeting data. The result could resemble the webbed dome of protection once confined to science fiction.

Unarmed variants could deliver blood, medicine, water-purification supplies, food and communications equipment after disasters. Drones already transport vaccines, blood products and diagnostic samples to remote regions, while companies test food and package delivery. A national drone reserve could strengthen military defense and disaster response.

comments.name: Midwest
comments.body: Ruth Franklin should be congratulated for this extremely wise, sensitive, and intellectually stimulating essay -- one of the very best I have ever read in the NYT. I am saying this as someone who does humanities scholarship for a living. Huckleberry Finn is, with Moby Dick, the greatest American novel of the 19th century, precisely for the reasons that come out in the piece. I especially appreciated the detailed attention to the writerly, formal aspects of narrative voice. Twain was a master of that, and much hangs in the balance with his ironic slides between Jim and Huck, as well as within Huck himself. I fully understand why readers are shocked by some of the language, but agree that Twain is placing that language in Huck's mouth both as a way to critique social violence that underlies casual indifference. This critical purchase on one's own assumption -- the growth that Huck experiences -- is all due to Jim. He is the moral compass of the book. Even so, it is understandable that Black readers will experience the book, at its best, as carrying a lesson that they do not themselves need to learn. That's of course right. But we all have an interest in each other's freedom and, since humans are inherently social and dependent on one another -- that means an interest in foster in each other -- Black or white -- mutual understanding. We need solidarity balanced with respect for our many differences. It strikes me that the novel will always have a role to play in showing that

comments.name: Metrowest Mom

I introduced the unit with a discussion of "that word," asking my students for their views on saying it aloud.  (A very lively discussion also came about in response to Professor's Gribben's suggestion that "slave" should replace the offending noun.)  As we examined the Biblical references, the over-the-top Royal Nonesuch, that heart-wrenching story of Lizabeth, Tom's position - in Huck's eyes - as "the cool kid," and Jim's ultimate persistence as the real father/hero of the story, my students got to see and talk about issues and challenges they continue to encounter today.  Looking back, my big regret is that Percival Everett's brilliant "James" arrived several years after I retired.  How I would have loved teaching these two extraordinary novels, together!

The only reason classical music has deified its interpreters (performers) and teachers of interpretations is that until recently, composers did not have the technology, the tools as the other arts had, to create their one product from their unique inspiration. They didn’t have their slab of granite or palette of colors. They could only leave instructions – notes, speed, rhythm, volume, cues to expressiveness, instrumentation – for others to follow. In other words, we've all been deluded to think that a piece of music exists only in someone's interpretation, not in itself.

If Guillaume Dufay and Josquin des Prez or the creators of Gregorian Chant had had tape recorders, we would now have a conception of music that was parallel universe-different from the historical one. We would all be listening to the one recording of Bach’s Mass in B minor and Chopin’s Barcarolle, produced by those geniuses themselves; buying or hearing in museums facsimiles of the one rare masterpiece. Pianists and flutists and clarinetists and conductors would be rid of their pretensions and off their cushioned butts, happy to be composing and teaching. comments.body: I work as a studio producer and producer of albums in Berkeley and have a whole bunch of young musicians, engineers and songwriters coming through on a weekly basis. I would agree, don't make Gods out of those that have succeeded. Much of music's success is due to marketing anyways - not necessarily the music itself - and we now live in a world over-run by 24-7, lowest common denominator marketing that puts music on the same level as a new item at Taco Bell. Trump imposed sweeping tariffs under one theory and lost. He then turned to Section 122 of the Trade Act. The Court of International Trade ruled those tariffs unlawful, and his administration is now appealing while offering a new economic rationale.

We have seen the same pattern with the White House ballroom. Two lower courts concluded Trump lacked authority to proceed without congressional approval, yet Chief Justice Roberts temporarily allowed construction to continue while the Supreme Court considers the case.

Enough. The judiciary is not the President’s appeals department, and the Constitution does not give him unlimited retries until he finds an argument that works. Congress legislates. Courts interpret the law.

The author writes: "If we do nothing, starving A.I. chatbots may be left with nothing to eat but their own responses."

The essay says, "Affirming those copyright protections to include A.I. might even force A.I. companies to hire human writers to create original works for their L.L.M.s to train on." 

L.L.M.s are already trained in part by writers hired by A.I. companies who may pose hypothetical questions to the models, provide feedback and corrections regarding answers generated by the models, and more. 

I would also point out that every writer worth his or her salt owes something to what others have written.  The fiction writer may be inspired by numerous novels and short stories written over the years. The non-fiction writer may rely even more directly on an assortment of books and articles relevant to the topic on which they are writing. Few if any writers operate in a complete vacuum. The difference between human writers and L.L.M.s is that  presumably the humans have bought and paid for some of the books and articles on which they have been "trained." And at least in the case of non-fiction, human writers are more likely to cite their sources.

comments.body: Martin Frankel was convicted of fraud based on a very similar fact pattern.  The parallels between Martin Frankel and the situation now surrounding Mark Walter are difficult to ignore. Frankel gained control of insurance companies and improperly used their assets to finance his own interests. His conduct was unquestionably illegal and ultimately resulted in criminal convictions. The allegations being investigated in the Mark Walter matter raise a strikingly similar concern: insurance companies under Walter’s control made billions of dollars in loans that ultimately benefited businesses connected to Walter, while approximately $21 billion of those investments were later reclassified as related-party transactions. If investigators establish that intermediaries were deliberately used to conceal the true related-party nature of those loans from regulators, that would not simply be aggressive financial engineering—it could constitute illegal fraud. The fact that Walter is scrambling to unload assets and repay loans is very telling.

Berkshire Hathaway was built upon using cheap insurance company "float" to invest in other assets.  The Dodgers acquisition was investigated years ago and apparently there was nothing wrong with it.  Sports franchises have been great investments in the past couple of decades.  Walter's investments can probably be sold for a lot more than what was paid for them, as illustrated by the recent Lakers sale.  I can only imagine (and be jealous of) what the Dodgers must be worth today compared to what Walter and his partners  paid for the team years ago.   Thus it does not seem very likely that any policyholder's money has been lost, and hopefully regulators and law enforcement authorities will not cause it to be lost.  Not that it is any of my business, but I think Walter must be given the opportunity to explain what he has done.  He will probably have to explain matters to regulators and legal authorities, and he isn't likely to talk to the press or the public while investigations are ongoing, and maybe he never will, since his business is his business and not the public's.  We will all have to wait for another day before hearing the final chapter on Mark Walter, but it doesn't seem like this is that big of a case.

I graduated into the Ford-Carter doldrums with an English major, but eventually made a career in media. And there remains an argument for studying what you love, then figuring out how to make money with it. 

The affordability issue, in academia as well as private industry, is income inequality. Administrators' and head coaches' salaries, lavish Taj Mahal construction projects, etc. are where a lot of that money now goes, while students are taught by embarrassingly low-paid adjuncts and grad students doing piece work. The 2023 Canadian wildfires released more CO2 than the rest of Canadian sources combined (37 million acres burned). Climate models did not project fires like that until much later this century.

And recently this paper reported that the permafrost region has shifted from an important carbon sink into a net emitter of greenhouse gases, CO2 and methane.

Some natural systems like forests and frozen soils which minimized some of the impacts of our atmospheric experiment with our only planet are changing from being our friends to our enemies.

My comment is a nit, but one which 99% of journalists get wrong: grain is not stored in silos, it is stored in grain bins and grain elevators.  If it's a major transshipment point it may be referred to as a grain terminal.  A silo has an entirely different function, that is to store green fodder crops in anaerobic conditions where it will ferment and become highly nutritious livestock feed, or silage.  In my life I have operated combines harvesting small grains, and forage harvesters chopping corn for silage, they each have their storage facilities and they are definitely not interchangeable. I dug out of storage a rebounder I had given my parents 20 years ago. Every time I visited I had her sit at the edge of her bed with her feet on the trampoline mat while I bounced for a few minutes. We noticed that after I visited and made her do this that her urine volume quadrupled that night. The aides always measured this when they emptied the bag from her catheter. With this evidence of improvement the aides began doing the rebounding sessions with her when i was not there. These rebounding sessions kept her from holding fluid in her legs, and kept her hip knee and ankle joints mobile. I believe that they also helped her kidneys regain their full function. Once we found the miracle of eating a single oyster each day, her wound began healing at warp speed. The wound nurses who came twice a week to measure and clean it could not believe their eyes. Now my mom is out of the bed, walking with a walker, and getting back to her busy social life. She still rebounds with me and her number one aide. comments.body: Not sure anything planted near Ground Zero is such a good idea. In addition to the fungal pathogens, there's all the pollutants found near the site that have proven to be carcinogenic -- even years later, resulting in fatalities.

articles.title: A Tree With Ties to Anne Frank Struggles to Survive
articles.summary: The tree, grown from a cutting of the Anne Frank tree in Amsterdam, is planted across from ground zero.

articles.title: The Ruthless Efficiency of Ultrapotent Street Drugs
articles.summary: Five decades after the “war on drugs” sought to make substance abuse unaffordable, illicit drugs are cheaper and more powerful than ever. A visit to Baltimore shows why.
